e-8177.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given Old Variables Through New Variables
e-8177.problem: Given that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066712/assets/57718ef2e6ecd26138c4c6a1b817d1129ad95a7473bf2e7d1611fdc64391e5c8.png) express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2-x_2^2\,$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$
e-8177.worked_solution:
First, notice that  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066712/assets/12e6df2cc03a95228ac8d54512772c914f3283f1f62d814f2e996de67c93a041.png)

gives the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{1}-{y}_{2})^{2}-(2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

e-8178.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given New Variables Through Old Variables
e-8178.problem: Given that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066712/assets/309c32ea89b3e3216e79962d305ef2611eeb691342ae07f7659aff52c218c5b3.png) express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1x_2+2x_2^2$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$
e-8178.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066712/assets/7ea02af91b7b066c7aafa293882f6e2f9f81256fe8b0a30f33f2f4403142d928.png) 

gives the following expressions for $y_1$ and $y_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for $x_1$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{2})(-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})+2(-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{2}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{1}^{2}+9{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+10{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

e-8179.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
e-8179.problem:
Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ below. Find the matrix of the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066712/assets/8c8f1626eafc81b4700a0ddc015c210508d4db464970abc706831ea86659e8da.png)
e-8179.worked_solution:
Recall that if $\mathbf{x}=[x_1, x_2]^T$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $\mathbf{y}=[ y_1, y_2 ]^T$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The matrix gives x_1=2y_1 and x_2=y_1+2y_2. Substituting, Q=-4y_1^2+6y_1(y_1+2y_2)-2(y_1+2y_2)^2=4y_1y_2-8y_2^2, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

  

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-(2{y}_{1})^{2}+3(2{y}_{1})({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})-2({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =-4{y}_{1}^{2}+6{y}_{1}^{2}+12{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-2{y}_{1}^{2}-8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Given that [x1x2]=[2012][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=−x12+3x1x2−2x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
y12+4y1y2−y22
b
y12−2y1y2−3y22
c
y12−y22
d
4y1y2−8y22
e
y1y2−y12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[x1x2]=[2012][y1y2]

gives the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=2y1x2=y1+2y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=−x12+3x1x2−2x22=−(2y1)2+3(2y1)(y1+2y2)−2(y1+2y2)2=−4y12+6y12+12y1y2−2y12−8y1y2−8y22=4y1y2−8y22

content.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given Old Variables Through New Variables
content.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

  

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-(2{y}_{1})^{2}+3(2{y}_{1})({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})-2({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =-4{y}_{1}^{2}+6{y}_{1}^{2}+12{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-2{y}_{1}^{2}-8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 2
?

Given that [x1x2]=[2−112][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12+x1x2−3x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
4y12−y1y2−6y22
b
3y12−13y1y2−13y22
c
2y12+y1y2−3y22
d
7y12−17y1y2−12y22
e
7y12−y1y2+3y22
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[x1x2]=[2−112][y1y2]

gives the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=2y1−y2x2=y1+2y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=2x12+x1x2−3x22=2(2y1−y2)2+(2y1−y2)(y1+2y2)−3(y1+2y2)2=8y12−8y1y2+2y22+2y12+3y1y2−2y22−3y12−12y1y2−12y22=7y12−17y1y2−12y22

verification.explanation: Substituting x_1=2y_1-y_2 and x_2=y_1+2y_2 gives coefficients 8+2-3=7, -8+3-12=-17, and 2-2-12=-12. Therefore option d matches both the direct calculation and the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

Question 3
?

Given that [x1x2]=[510−2][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x1x2−2x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
25y12−9y22
b
−y12+12y1y2+3y22
c
5y12−10y1y2
d
25y12+10y1y2+y22
e
y1y2+y22
Submit

decision.explanation: The matrix gives x_1=5y_1+y_2 and x_2=-2y_2. Substituting yields Q=(5y_1+y_2)^2-2y_2(5y_1+y_2)-8y_2^2=25y_1^2-9y_2^2, which is option a.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

  

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =5{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(5{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2}+(5{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})(-2{y}_{2})-2(-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =25{y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =25{y}_{1}^{2}-9{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that [x1x2]=[510−2][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x1x2−2x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
25y12−9y22
b
−y12+12y1y2+3y22
c
5y12−10y1y2
d
25y12+10y1y2+y22
e
y1y2+y22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[x1x2]=[510−2][y1y2]

gives the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=5y1+y2x2=−2y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12+x1x2−2x22=(5y1+y2)2+(5y1+y2)(−2y2)−2(−2y2)2=25y12+10y1y2+y22−10y1y2−2y22−8y22=25y12−9y22

content.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given Old Variables Through New Variables
content.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

  

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =5{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(5{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2}+(5{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})(-2{y}_{2})-2(-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =25{y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =25{y}_{1}^{2}-9{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Given that [x1x2]=[11−11][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
2y12+4y2y1−y22
b
y12−4y2y1+y22
c
y12−y22
d
2y12+2y22
e
y12+4y2y1
Submit

decision.explanation: The matrix gives x_1=y_1+y_2 and x_2=-y_1+y_2. Hence Q=(y_1+y_2)^2+(-y_1+y_2)^2=2y_1^2+2y_2^2, since the cross terms cancel.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2}+(-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

Given that [x1x2]=[11−11][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
2y12+4y2y1−y22
b
y12−4y2y1+y22
c
y12−y22
d
2y12+2y22
e
y12+4y2y1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[x1x2]=[11−11][y1y2]

gives the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=y1+y2x2=−y1+y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12+x22=(y1+y2)2+(−y1+y2)2=y12+2y1y2+y22+y12−2y1y2+y22=2y12+2y22

verification.explanation: With x_1=y_1+y_2 and x_2=-y_1+y_2, Q=(y_1+y_2)^2+(-y_1+y_2)^2=2y_1^2+2y_2^2. This confirms option d and agrees with the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given Old Variables Through New Variables
content.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2}+(-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Given that [x1x2]=[10−13][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−4x1x2+3x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
4y12−3y1y2+9y22
b
y12+12y1y2−9y22
c
y12−4y1y2+3y22
d
8y12−30y1y2+27y22
e
8y12−15y1y2−27y22
Submit

decision.explanation: The matrix gives x_1=y_1 and x_2=-y_1+3y_2. Substituting gives Q=y_1^2-4y_1(-y_1+3y_2)+3(-y_1+3y_2)^2=8y_1^2-30y_1y_2+27y_2^2, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$

Question 5
?

Given that [x1x2]=[10−13][y1y2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−4x1x2+3x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
4y12−3y1y2+9y22
b
y12+12y1y2−9y22
c
y12−4y1y2+3y22
d
8y12−30y1y2+27y22
e
8y12−15y1y2−27y22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[x1x2]=[10−13][y1y2]

gives the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=y1x2=−y1+3y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12−4x1x2+3x22=(y1)2−4(y1)(−y1+3y2)+3(−y1+3y2)2=y12+4y12−12y1y2+3y12−18y1y2+27y22=8y12−30y1y2+27y22

Question 6
?

Given that [y1y2]=[31−10][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+4x1x2 in terms of the components of y.

a
8y22−8y1y2
b
−11y22−4y1y2
c
−12y22−2y1y2
d
−9y12−4y1y2
e
−12y12−4y1y2
Submit

decision.explanation: The equations are y_1=3x_1+x_2 and y_2=-x_1, so x_1=-y_2 and x_2=y_1+3y_2. Therefore Q=(-y_2)^2+4(-y_2)(y_1+3y_2)=-11y_2^2-4y_1y_2, matching option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{2})^{2}+4(-{y}_{2})({y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}) \\  & ={y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-12{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-11{y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 6
?

Given that [y1y2]=[31−10][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+4x1x2 in terms of the components of y.

a
8y22−8y1y2
b
−11y22−4y1y2
c
−12y22−2y1y2
d
−9y12−4y1y2
e
−12y12−4y1y2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[y1y2]=[31−10][x1x2]

gives the following expressions for y1 and y2:

y1=3x1+x2y2=−x1

By solving the second equation for x1 and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=−y2x2=y1+3y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12+4x1x2=(−y2)2+4(−y2)(y1+3y2)=y22−4y1y2−12y22=−11y22−4y1y2

content.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given New Variables Through Old Variables
content.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{2})^{2}+4(-{y}_{2})({y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}) \\  & ={y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-12{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-11{y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Given that [y1y2]=[−10−21][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−6x1x2+x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
−7y12+2y1y2+y22
b
y12+2y1y2+y22
c
−6y12−2y1y2+y22
d
5y12+2y1y2−y22
e
7y12−2y1y2−y22
Submit

decision.explanation: The equations y_1=-x_1 and y_2=-2x_1+x_2 give x_1=-y_1 and x_2=y_2-2y_1. Substituting yields Q=y_1^2-6(-y_1)(y_2-2y_1)+(y_2-2y_1)^2=-7y_1^2+2y_1y_2+y_2^2, matching option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} & =-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the first equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & =-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{1})^{2}-6(-{y}_{1})(-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})+(-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-12{y}_{1}^{2}+6{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+4{y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Given that [y1y2]=[−10−21][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−6x1x2+x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
−7y12+2y1y2+y22
b
y12+2y1y2+y22
c
−6y12−2y1y2+y22
d
5y12+2y1y2−y22
e
7y12−2y1y2−y22
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[y1y2]=[−10−21][x1x2]

gives the following expressions for y1 and y2:

y1=−x1y2=−2x1+x2

By solving the first equation for x1 and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=−y1x2=−2y1+y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12−6x1x2+x22=(−y1)2−6(−y1)(−2y1+y2)+(−2y1+y2)2=y12−12y12+6y1y2+4y12−4y1y2+y22=−7y12+2y1y2+y22

verification.explanation: Using x_1=-y_1 and x_2=-2y_1+y_2, expansion gives Q=(1-12+4)y_1^2+(6-4)y_1y_2+y_2^2=-7y_1^2+2y_1y_2+y_2^2. This confirms option a and agrees with the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given New Variables Through Old Variables
content.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} & =-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the first equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & =-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{1})^{2}-6(-{y}_{1})(-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})+(-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-12{y}_{1}^{2}+6{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+4{y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

Given that [y1y2]=[10−1−1][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+5x1x2−x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
2y12−5y1y2−y22
b
−5y12−7y1y2−y22
c
−2y12+4y1y+y22
d
−3y12−9y1y2−y22
e
5y12−6y1y2+y22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[y1y2]=[10−1−1][x1x2]

gives the following expressions for y1 and y2:

y1=x1y2=−x1−x2

By solving the first equation for x1 and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=y1x2=−y1−y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12+5x1x2−x22=y12+5y1(−y1−y2)−(−y1−y2)2=y12−5y12−5y1y2−y12−2y1y2−y22=−5y12−7y1y2−y22

Question 9
?

Given that [y1y2]=[−21−10][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12+x1x2−x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
y12−4y1y2+4y22
b
−y12+3y1y2
c
y12+5y1y2
d
−y12+3y1y2+8y22
e
y12+4y1y2−8y22
Submit

decision.explanation: Since y_2=-x_1 and y_1=-2x_1+x_2, we have x_1=-y_2 and x_2=y_1-2y_2. Therefore Q=2y_2^2-y_2(y_1-2y_2)-(y_1-2y_2)^2=-y_1^2+3y_1y_2, matching option b.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}-2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2(-{y}_{2})^{2}+(-{y}_{2})({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})-({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-4{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{y}_{1}^{2}+3{y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

Given that [y1y2]=[−21−10][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12+x1x2−x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
y12−4y1y2+4y22
b
−y12+3y1y2
c
y12+5y1y2
d
−y12+3y1y2+8y22
e
y12+4y1y2−8y22
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[y1y2]=[−21−10][x1x2]

gives the following expressions for y1 and y2:

y1=−2x1+x2y2=−x1

By solving the second equation for x1 and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=−y2x2=y1−2y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=2x12+x1x2−x22=2(−y2)2+(−y2)(y1−2y2)−(y1−2y2)2=2y22−y2y1+2y22−y12+4y1y2−4y22=−y12+3y1y2

verification.explanation: Substituting x_1=-y_2 and x_2=y_1-2y_2 gives Q=2y_2^2-y_1y_2+2y_2^2-y_1^2+4y_1y_2-4y_2^2=-y_1^2+3y_1y_2. This confirms option b and matches the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option d.

content.knowledge_point: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given New Variables Through Old Variables
content.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}-2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2(-{y}_{2})^{2}+(-{y}_{2})({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})-({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-4{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{y}_{1}^{2}+3{y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The equations give x_2=-y_2 and x_1=-y_1+y_2. Substituting yields Q=(-y_1+y_2)^2-2(-y_1+y_2)(-y_2)-4y_2^2=y_1^2-4y_1y_2-y_2^2, matching option e.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

 

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{2}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}-2({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})(-{y}_{2})-4(-{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-4{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Given that [y1y2]=[−1−10−1][x1x2], express the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−2x1x2−4x22 in terms of the components of y.

a
y12−2y1y2−y22
b
2y12−4y1y2+y22
c
y12+4y1y2+2y22
d
−2y1y2−6y22
e
y12−4y1y2−y22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[y1y2]=[−1−10−1][x1x2]

gives the following expressions for y1 and y2:

y1=−x1−x2y2=−x2

By solving the second equation for x2 and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for x1 and x2:

x1=−y1+y2x2=−y2

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

Q(x)=x12−2x1x2−4x22=(y2−y1)2−2(y2−y1)(−y2)−4(−y2)2=y22−2y1y2+y12+2y22−2y1y2−4y22=y12−4y1y2−y22

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & -14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that if x=[x1,x2]T is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and y=[y1,y2]T is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of P, then

x=Py.

As a result, we have

xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=(yTPT)A(Py)=yT(PTAP)y,

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

PTAP=[1−211]T[−1332][1−211]=[11−21][−1332][1−211]=[255−4][1−211]=[711−14]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & -14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}19 & 9 \\ 9 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}19 & 9 \\ 9 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that if x=[x1,x2]T is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and y=[y1,y2]T is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of P, then

x=Py.

As a result, we have

xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=(yTPT)A(Py)=yT(PTAP)y,

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

PTAP=[1−121]T[2113][1−121]=[12−11][2113][1−121]=[47−12][1−121]=[18333]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 13 \\ 13 & 14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & -13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & -13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
